questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: What motivated me was to explore new cultures, but in an enviroment close to home. My aim was to make connections from all over the world, which exchange gives a great opportunity to do!

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Since I have earlier had problems with home sickness it was important for me to choose a country with a similar culture to mine. However I still wanted to explore something new, so I chose a destination where I knew that was possible. Since I am from Denmark, Norway was the perfect destination for that. The culture (and language) is similar, but the nature is so different and beautiful.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I went on exchange at the University of Oslo. They have a great website with all the information about what you need to do before you enter Norway and when you arrive in Norway. They have guides on how to apply and so on, and they even have a packing list and a video showing how to dress like a real norwegian. I went there during the autumn semester and got to experience three very different seasons with weather from 25 celcius degrees to -10 celcius degrees. However, it was more tricky to find information about the COVID-19 situation, since they announce the new restrictions and so on with very short warning. So a good advice is to stay updated everyday.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The university arranges a buddy week (introduction/orientation week) in the week before the semester starts. In this week we did a lot of social stuff like barbequeing, trips and games. This created a good foundation for new friendships and it was an easy way to meet new people. During this week we also got a tour around the campus, information about the university and activities you can do besides your studies. We also had a small sightseeing in Oslo.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: For me it was easy to find housing. When you study in Oslo (at any university) you can apply for housing at SIO. They have different student houses and villages around the city. Under normal circumstances SIO offers student housing to every exchange students. During the pandemic however it has not been possible for them to guarantee housing, which this semester led a lot of students without housing. My advice is therefore to apply as early as possible and apply for the bigger student villages like Sogn and Kringsjå. I would also apply for private student housing like Anker, which is a bit more expensive but located in the city center. Maybe it is also an idea to check out the private market. The reason that SIO could not provide housing for all the exchange students is because the Norwegian student, due to corona, not have been able to go on exchange and lent our their rooms. At least not as many as normally.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I was super happy with living in Kringsjå. The T-bane (metro) goes directly to the university and if you like walking, it does not take longer than 30-40 minutes to walk to the university. Kringsjå is 6 km from the city center, but not longer away than that you can take T-bane (during the day) or night buses (during the night in weekends). The transport has not been a problem to me. Kringsjå is located right next to a beautiful lake called Sognsvann where you can swim in the summer and (if the weather allows it) skate in the winter. From Sognsvann there a many different hiking routes, so a perfect place to go on adventure. If you are lucky you might even see the northern lights from there. In Kringsjå you find a big and cheap supermarket (Kiwi), a fitness center and a cafe. SIO owns both the fitness and the cafe which makes the prices very student friendly.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Living at SIO gives a lot of advangeges. In the beginning of the semester they arrange a reuse festival where you can be lucky to find a piece of furniture (or two) for your room for free. Besides that they make events every week throughout the semester around in Oslo. Examples are karaoke night, outdoor cinema, speed friending, trips to the cinema (for free) and quiz nights.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to register for courses in a program called Studentweb. Here you also find your dates of exams, grades and so on later in the semester. You choose courses of 30 credits in total and wait and hope to get the ones you have registered for. If you do not get accepted to the course you wanted you will have another opportunity to apply for the courses that are still available.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: At the website of the University of Oslo it is possible to find guides that explains how to register.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: The courses are not present in studentweb all at once (some are shown later than others). This meant that when I wanted to register for courses I could not find all the courses I wanted. The University of Oslo recommended me to apply as soon as possible for courses to be sure to get the ones I wanted. So to be sure to get the two courses I found a third course that was not my first priority, but ok, and registered for all at ones.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The registration period is long which makes it possible to wait for all your wanted courses to show, but it will decrease your chances of getting in. Therefore I would advice to do what I did and apply as soon as possible so that you are sure to get at least some of the courses you want. I ended up finding the last course very fun and interesting, even though it was not what I wanted to begin with.  Also, use the website of the University of Oslo! A lot of help is to be found there!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Two out of three courses were a mix of bachelor and master students. However I did not find it hard to follow the classes. The difference between thoses courses and the course with only bachelor students is that the two mixed courses were more specified on a subject as fx Henrik Ibsen or time in audiovisual media. I found the level very similar to the courses at the University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching was very similar compared to UCPH. In one of my courses we had lectures once a week where we learned about a topic and a seminar the day after where we talk more about a specific text or film related to that topic. The other courses consisted only of seminars, which I have not yet experienced at the UCPH, however I do believe that this kind of structure exists as well. However one thing differs. Eventhough all of my three course were 10 credits, two of them only lasted half a semester. This reminds a bit of a block structure.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I was enrolled the three following courses: 
MEVIT1110 -  Audiovisual Aesthetics 
MEVIT3529 -  Audiovisual Media Temporalities: Temporality in Films, Series, Games and Social Media 
IBS2105 - Ibsen Between Cultures

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was in generel happy with all three courses, but I would mostly recommend the course MEVIT1110 - Audiovisual Aesthetics. It is perfect if you are interested in film or media in generel. At each lecture we started out learning about a specific term like mise-en-scene, different forms of editing and so on. After an hour we would watch a movie and then end with a small lecture about that specific movie. The day after we would have a seminar where we practised using what we learned about the day before. A very well structured and relaxing course, but also the course where I learned the most.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Your new friends probably want to travel around all of Norway with you, so make sure to save up some money for this! I spent around 3000 DKK but depending on how many places you want to visit the expenses can go up or down.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food in Norway is in generel a bit more expensive than in Denmark. However it you go to the right stores (Kiwi and Rema 1000) it is possible to find good deals and cheap brands. The alcohol is way more expensive. In supermarkets it is possible to find beers for a good price but if you go to a bar the cheapest beer can easily be three times as expensive as a cheap beer in Denmark. A good advice is therefore to use the student bars. Museums and similar activities often have a great student discount, which makes it possible to experience cultural things while you are away. A good advice is just to expect everything to be a bit more expensive, look for the discounts and make use of SIO free events.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: SIO have fitness centers around in Oslo, one located on campus. Not far from campus is another fitness center with swimming pool and tennis and badminton courts that you can book. In the beginning of the semester the university will arrange association days where you can learn about all the different associations. A few examples of associations are choir, outdoor, knitting, d&d and way more! There is definitely something for everyone. At campus they have lots of cafes and places to eat (with vegan options as well). Not far from campus is a place called Chau de Neuf which is a bar for students. Here they throw parties, concerts and make other events. On campus they also have a lot of student driven bars and if you want to get cheaper drinks you can become a volunteer here. In the beginning of the semester SIO arrange a weekend where you can get free tickets to different activities around the city. This semester it included trips to a theme park, SUP boarding, a guided tour in the opera house and way more.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you like sports and outdoor I would recommend to go hiking in the mountains around Sognsvann, or other places outside of Oslo. If you do not like outdoor but does like sport I would recommend joining the gym (Athletica). They have lots of centers around the city and a very student friendly price of only 205 NOK pr month. This give you acces to group sessions, the swimming pool, the badminton and tennis court and all the centers. I would also recommend keeping an eye of the events that SIO arrange (perhaps on their facebook or instagram). It is cheap and you meet a lot of other students. A good way to meet other students is to join an association - especially because you here meet people with the same interests as you.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would recommend them to go hiking! The nature is so beautiful and looks different everytime you go out. If possible take a trip to another city in Norway like Bergen, Trondheim or Stavanger. I was in Tromsø and it was the greatest and most beautiful experience of my life. Also, I recommend to go to a student bar and get a feeling of the student life in Oslo. And of course, go on a sightseeing in Oslo cause they have some beautiful attractions like the opera house, the new munch museum and the royal palace.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: My feeling is that the people in Norway are very similar to the people in Denmark. Besides that the culture is also very similar, and this made it easy to adjust. I have a few norwegian friends in Oslo from earlier so for me it was easy to understand norwegian. My experience however is that even though you do not feel comfortable with the norwegian language before, you will learn it very quick.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Since I already knew some students in Oslo it was easy for me to meet more local students. If you do not know anyone beforehand I will recommend to join associations, try to socialize during seminars (there will always be norwegian students in your class) or volunteer at the student bars.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find anything challenging regarding cultural differences, since the differences are very small

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciated how the norwegian students reminds me a lot about the danish students.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Explore the nature, take part in SIOs events and be open to new experiences

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Enjoy your stay, time will go fast!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience is my new friendships. It is so interesting to meet and be a part of all these different cultures!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: At the University of Copenhagen all my courses are in danish, so the biggest challenge for me was to suddenly have lectures and seminars in english - and especially exams!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
